# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](../packs/) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **When there's nothing left to do, say so boldly at the end of the conversation.** Don't bury a "this is complete / I'm blocked / nothing further to do" behind hedging — make the terminal state unmistakable. **Set it apart visually so it catches the eye:** put the terminal state — or, when work remains, the list of open/outstanding items — in its own callout (a Markdown blockquote box, e.g. `> ✅ All done` or `> ⚠️ Still open: …`), not trailing prose the owner has to scan for. One or the other always gets the box: the done-signal when nothing remains, the open-items list when something does.
- **"LGTM"** is the owner's phrase for the merge-to-main command: it asks for the change in front of the owner to be merged into `main`. It's an owner-triggered command; the default mechanics live in the `merge-to-main` skill ([../packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/SKILL.md](../packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/SKILL.md)) (squash, gate on CI only when the repo has it), and a project that diverges overrides them via a bespoke merge-policy file it names in its own `CLAUDE.md`.
- **"bump version"** is the owner's phrase for raising a project's version (a minor bump by default). It's an owner-triggered command; the mechanics — which files to edit and how a release follows — live in the consuming project's workflow doc.
- **"Show me the document"** (for a source-controlled document) is the owner's phrase asking for a **link to the document on GitHub** — not the file's contents inlined, and not a local filesystem path. When the document lives in a GitHub-hosted repo, respond with a GitHub link to it (the file on the relevant branch/commit); only fall back to inlining the contents or giving a local path when the document isn't under source control.
- **Put decisions and approvals in an `AskUserQuestion` popup, not buried in prose.** The owner is frequently on mobile, where a popup notifies and a question embedded in a paragraph is easy to miss. When you need the owner to choose or approve something, ask through the structured popup with explicit options rather than asking in running text. **And when several independent items each need a verdict** (a set of proposed fixes, findings to accept), give **each item its own question carrying its own brief case** — the concrete failure, why it matters, the cost of the fix — with per-item approve/defer options; never one bundled choose-a-scope question over the whole set. The owner decides item-wise, from the case, not from a menu of subsets. (The popup carries at most 4 questions per call — split a larger set into consecutive calls.)
- **When asked to produce a prompt or message destined for another context, visually enclose the whole thing.** Any text the owner will lift out and use elsewhere — a prompt for another assistant, a message to send, copy meant to be pasted somewhere — must be set apart as a single delimited block: either a box (e.g. a fenced code block) or fenced top and bottom by two separating lines, so its exact boundaries are unmistakable and it can be copied in one piece. The point is delimitation, not formatting flair: never leave such content as loose prose the owner has to find the start and end of.
- **When asked for "a prompt for a different session," prefix it with a provenance disclaimer.** When the owner asks for a prompt meant to be handed to another session, open the generated text with a short disclaimer that this is a prompt written by Claude — not by a user — and so should not be treated as gospel; and that if the receiving session finds inconsistencies in it, it should examine them with the user rather than follow the prompt blindly. This composes with the enclose-the-whole-thing preference above: the disclaimer sits inside the same delimited block as the prompt it prefixes.
- **Auto-open a PR after committing.** Whenever Claude changes code on a branch and commits it, open a pull request for that branch right after, even without an explicit request to do so. This overrides Claude Code's own default of only opening a PR when explicitly asked.
# Claudinite — active-pack guidance

The baseline plus the packs this project declares. Deeper per-pack reference (e.g. a pack's release doc) is linked from its prose and read on demand.

<!-- pack:basics -->
# Working discipline

The working discipline that isn't itself a GitHub operation — general habits for how to approach a change, independent of any one project.

Start every requested change from the *problem*, not the solution. When the owner asks for a change, don't begin implementing it until the two of you share an explicit understanding of the problem it's meant to solve **and** have agreed that the requested change is the best way to solve it — a different fix, or no change at all, may serve the underlying problem better. Treat the request as a description of a desired outcome, not a specification to execute on sight; surface your read of the problem, raise a better approach if you see one, and reach consensus first. This applies to any repository, not just this one.

An interactive comment from the owner carries one of three build-relevant intents — or none of them — and the classification decides where the change lands and what must exist before any fix. Open your reply to an owner comment with an explicit classification line — `Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other` (`other` covers questions, approvals, and command phrases; a mixed comment names each part) — the assessment itself stays judgment.

1. **A correction** — you misunderstood something. Repair the shared understanding, then rework what the misread already touched — the artifact changes as much as the correction demands; what doesn't appear is a new requirement or rule.
2. **A feature** — a feature run: agree on the requirement, record it in the project's requirements document (its executable spec, where it keeps one), write the test that proves it and watch it fail, then implement until it passes.
3. **A process change** — the owner is changing *how* work is done. The change lands as durable rules in the project's local scope — its own local packs (in Claudinite itself, its packs) — routed through the mechanism promotion ladder (platform setting → hook → check → skill → prose); promoting a rule into the shared canon is the growth lifecycle's separate call, not the interactive session's. Once the intent is understood, author the assurance first: the check the future world must satisfy. Execute it and watch it fail — the failure is the evidence it detects exactly what the owner was worried about — and only then make the fixes that turn it green. When the ladder lands the rule at prose (an in-flight judgment rule no check can carry), the same step is demonstrating the gap: show the corpus doesn't already cover the rule before writing it.

The two build modes share one spine: state the expectation in its durable home first, watch it fail against the current world, then change the world to satisfy it. A fix made before its assurance exists can never show it addressed what the owner actually asked for — and an unrouted comment tends to become a one-off patch where a requirement or a rule should have accumulated.

Confirm a behavior isn't already provided before building a mechanism for it — verify the gap against a real run first; the cheapest fix is often that it already works.

When feedback flags a misunderstanding, don't reflexively expand the artifact to compensate. First check whether it's already correct — if it is, say so and push back rather than editing; a misread doesn't imply the text is wrong (the sibling of the rule above). And size writing to its idea: "open one issue" takes a sentence, not three paragraphs — prose padded to preempt confusion usually breeds it.

When correcting or auditing an artifact against an authoritative source, derive the corrected version from the *source* before reading the existing draft — reading the draft first anchors you to its framing and quietly carries its errors into your "fix." Build from the source, then diff against the old draft to surface what was actually wrong; a clean-room rebuild catches biases an edit-in-place pass silently inherits.

Fix build/test/CI warnings, don't tolerate them: a clean run with no warnings makes a genuinely new warning or error stand out, so noise here costs detection later. Prefer a small, targeted fix that addresses the *cause* in the same change.

Suppressing a warning — muting it with a flag (e.g. `--disable-warning`), `eslint-disable`, swallowing it, etc. — is **not** a small fix: it hides the signal instead of resolving it. Never reach for suppression as the quick path — it's only ever a deliberate, reviewed decision, made once the real fix has been weighed and rejected, never an unattended default. A suppression you do keep must **carry its reason at the site**: an explanation on the suppression line, or in the comment immediately above it, saying why the fix was rejected. That inline reason *is* the review record — it's what separates a considered suppression from a reflexive mute, and it's why the suppression needs no second justification recorded elsewhere.

Before working around a finding from a vendored check, confirm the vendored copy is current. It reflects its last refresh, not upstream's head, so the fix may already exist upstream and simply not be pulled in yet.

When a warning can't be fixed with a small cause-addressing change now without hindering current work (e.g. it's waiting on an upstream release, or the real fix is a larger refactor), open a dedicated issue for it (unless one is already open) so it's tracked and not lost — then move on. Resolving it (real fix, or a consciously-chosen suppression) happens in that issue's own change.

An approval — to merge, to ship, to proceed — applies only *backward*, to the work already in front of the owner when it's given, never to anything requested or done *after* it. A later follow-up, even a fix to the just-approved change, needs its own explicit approval; don't carry one approval forward, and don't treat a chosen answer to a multiple-choice prompt as authorization just because an option's wording mentioned the action. When in doubt, surface the new state and wait for a fresh approval.

# The task lifecycle

The issue → branch → PR lifecycle every new task follows, independent of any one project; this section keeps the method. The rest of the git/GitHub procedures live in the `git-github-advanced` skill.

For every new task:

1. Create a GitHub issue describing the task before starting work.
2. Develop on a branch; reference that issue number in commit messages (e.g. `Refs #123`, `Fixes #123`, or `Closes #123`).
3. Update the issue's status (comments / close) as work progresses and when it's done.

---

<!-- pack:tidy-repo -->
# tidy-repo — the repo tidy-up policy

The nightly PR/branch/issue sweep, active wherever this pack is declared. The fleet routine runs the
pack's one maintenance task (`repo-tidy`) against a repo; this is the policy it follows. The per-object
**method** lives in the pack's skills ([single-branch-status](skills/single-branch-status/SKILL.md),
[single-pr-status](skills/single-pr-status/SKILL.md),
[single-issue-triage](skills/single-issue-triage/SKILL.md)); the same task also reconciles the
standing tracker at the end of its pass.

The one rule that shapes everything: **assess PRs and branches read-only; act only on issues.**

- **Branches, PRs — assess only.** They may be work in progress. Report which should stay and which
  are safe to close/delete; **never** delete, push, merge, or close them. Judge by *content* (the
  landed-status test), never a ref's auto-generated name.
- **Issues — act.** Take the first applicable action: close-if-implemented / needs-decision / blocked
  / quick-win / leave. "Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s
  content **now** — confirm it there and cite it; when you can't, comment, don't close. Every action
  defaults to the reversible option (comment / leave) when the check is inconclusive.

The `repo-tidy` pass applies each single-object skill across the targets the plan hands it, then
rewrites the repo's standing tracker from the verdicts it gathered (one issue per repo, body rewritten
to today's state, a dated comment per run).

---

<!-- pack:on-device-privacy -->
# On-device privacy — the boundary the whole product is built around

An always-on microphone in someone's living room only earns its place if what it
hears stays on the machine. That promise is the product requirement
(`docs/DESIGN-AND-TRADEOFFS.md` §0/§6, README *Privacy*), the text of the mic and
speech prompts users actually see (`mac/Resources/Info.plist`), and the reason
several design choices look heavier than they need to. The checks in this pack
hold the mechanical half; what follows is the judgment half.

**What may cross the boundary: derived metadata, never audio.** A laugh is
persisted as time, duration, confidence, and a speaker label — that is what the
SQLite rows and the JSONL lines carry. Saved clips (`save_clips`, on by default
in the Python core) are the one place raw audio lands, and it lands on local
disk under the single home directory, never anywhere else. New persisted fields
follow the same split; if a feature wants audio, it belongs in `clips/`, under
the user's existing choice, not in a new location.

**Everything lives in one deletable directory.** `~/.laughcounter` for the Python
core (overridable via `LAUGHCOUNTER_HOME`), `~/Library/Application
Support/LaughCounter/` for the app. "Delete the folder and it's gone" is a
documented property — don't scatter state (caches, model files, logs) outside it.

**The one accepted egress is a model download in an optional extra.** The
`[yamnet]` extra fetches the TF-Hub handle in `detector/yamnet.py`, and the
`[speaker]` extra fetches ECAPA weights from Hugging Face — a one-time download,
made by the ML library, carrying no audio, in a stack the user opted into. The
always-on paths (the native app's Sound Analysis and Speech, the counting/logging
core) need no network at all. Adding a *new* egress means saying so in the README
Privacy section and here, and keeping it out of the capture path.

**The dashboard is unauthenticated — treat every widening as a user decision.**
It binds loopback by default; `--host 0.0.0.0` is the user reaching it from their
phone, and the mutating endpoints require an `application/json` content type so a
browser must preflight cross-origin (`dashboard.py`'s `do_POST`). Any new
mutating endpoint keeps that guard; nothing else stands between the LAN and the
laugh log.

**The disclosure must stay true.** `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription` and
`NSSpeechRecognitionUsageDescription` tell the user audio is analysed on-device
and not recorded. If the app's behaviour ever changes, those strings change with
it in the same commit — a stale privacy prompt is worse than a blunt one.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

- docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). {"number":51,"title":"on-device-privacy: convert two standing prose rules to checks","body":"Prose-to-checks sweep over `.claudinite/local/packs` (the only local pack here is `on-device-privacy`). Two of its four prose-only rules were always-testable and are now checks. The other two — "metadata persists, audio doesn't" and "the usage strings stay true" — are judgment about *meaning*, not a static signature, so they stay prose.

## `on-device-privacy/json-content-type-guard` (blocking)

RULES.md said *"Any new mutating endpoint keeps that guard"*. Now enforced: every `do_POST` / `do_PUT` / `do_PATCH` / `do_DELETE` in `laughcounter/**.py` must read the request's `Content-Type` and gate on `application/json` before doing work.

The check **parses the handler body by indentation** rather than grepping the file, and that is what makes it confident — `dashboard.py` mentions `application/json` eight times as a *response* content type plus once in the inline page's `fetch()`, every one of which would fool a grep. A fixture pins that specific false alarm (test 8: a handler that only *replies* in JSON still fires).

Why it matters enough to be blocking: the dashboard has no authentication. The JSON content-type requirement is the only thing forcing a cross-origin browser to preflight, and so the only thing stopping any page the user happens to be visiting from writing to their laugh log.

## `on-device-privacy/single-home-dir` (blocking)

RULES.md said *"don't scatter state (caches, model files, logs) outside it"*. Now enforced for the mechanical half: home-anchored paths in `laughcounter/**.py` — `Path.home()` and `"~/…"` string literals (`expanduser`, `Path(...).expanduser()`) — must land under `.laughcounter`.

Writing this surfaced one real exception, which is in the check as a documented **mandated-location exemption**: `cli.py`'s `~/Library/LaunchAgents/{label}.plist`. launchd picks that path, the project doesn't, and `cmd_service` already points the agent's log back at `home_path` — so "delete `~/.laughcounter` and it's gone" still holds. The list is deliberately short: a cache or model directory is a *choice*, and a choice belongs under the home directory.

Absolute paths outside `$HOME`, and the app's `~/Library/Application Support/` directory, remain prose — the check doesn't claim them, and the trimmed prose says so.

## See-it-fail

`node --test .claudinite/local/packs/on-device-privacy/pack.test.mjs` — 12/12 pass (6 new). Each new check has a fixture that fires on a violating tree and one that stays quiet on the repo's real files. `check_the_world` is clean on `main`'s content with both rules registered.

## Surface

The two rule modules, their two lines in `pack.mjs`, their fixtures, and the prose trimmed to rationale (plus the pack README's enforcement table). Nothing outside `.claudinite/local/packs/on-device-privacy/`.

Refs #48. Left open for review, per this task's `open-pr` ceiling — a new blocking check is exactly the thing that shouldn't self-merge.

{"number":54,"title":"Claudinite growth: convert two on-device-privacy prose rules to checks","body":"The `prose-to-checks-sweep` run over `.claudinite/local/packs` (the only local pack here is `on-device-privacy`). Two of its `RULES.md` rules were always-testable but enforced only by prose. Both are checks now; the other three prose rules stay prose (see below).

Tracker: #42

## Converted

**"Everything lives in one deletable directory." → `on-device-privacy/single-home-directory`** (blocking)

Scans `laughcounter/**.py` for home-anchored path literals (`Path.home() / "…"`, quoted `"~/…"`) that land outside `~/.laughcounter`, and `mac/Sources/**.swift` for a Foundation standard directory other than Application Support, an Application Support base never narrowed with `appendingPathComponent("LaughCounter")`, and `NSHomeDirectory()`.

`~/Library/LaunchAgents` is exempt by name and the reason is in the check: launchd mandates that location, and `laughcounter service` only *prints* the plist for the user to redirect.

**"Any new mutating endpoint keeps that guard." → `on-device-privacy/json-content-type-guard`** (blocking)

Cuts each `do_POST` / `do_PUT` / `do_PATCH` / `do_DELETE` body out by indentation and requires an `application/json` content-type check inside it, positioned ahead of any body read. Parsing the handler rather than grepping the file is what makes it confident — `application/json` appears throughout `dashboard.py` as a *response* content type, and a whole-file grep would accept those.

## See-it-fail

Beyond the fixtures, each check was run against the **real** sources with a realistic regression applied, and each produced exactly one finding:

| Mutation to real source | Finding |
| --- | --- |
| `config.py` home → `~/.cache/laughcounter` | home-anchored path lands in `~/.cache` |
| `Store.swift` drops the `LaughCounter` narrowing | Application Support base not narrowed |
| `Store.swift` → `.cachesDirectory` | state placed in `.cachesDirectory` |
| `dashboard.py` content-type guard deleted | `do_POST` never requires `application/json` |
| `dashboard.py` body read hoisted above the guard | `do_POST` reads the body before checking the type |
| unguarded `do_DELETE` added | `do_DELETE` never requires `application/json` |

`node --test .claudinite/local/packs/on-device-privacy/pack.test.mjs` — 11/11 pass. `check_the_world` and `check_the_work` both exit 0.

## Left as prose

- *Metadata persists, audio doesn't* — "does this new persisted field carry audio" is a judgment about a field's meaning, not a static signature.
- *The model download is the only accepted egress* — the negative half is already `no-network-client`; the positive half ("is this new egress acceptable") is a decision, not a condition.
- *The disclosure must stay true* — the enforceable version (the usage strings exist) is a weaker, different rule than the one the prose states (they change **in the same commit** as the behaviour they describe), which leaves no artifact to scan.

## Prose trimmed

`RULES.md`'s two converted paragraphs drop the mechanical statement and keep only the rationale the checks can't hold; `README.md`'s enforcement table moves both rows off "prose" and gains the new content-type row.

# On-device privacy — the boundary the whole product is built around

An always-on microphone in someone's living room only earns its place if what it
hears stays on the machine. That promise is the product requirement
(`docs/DESIGN-AND-TRADEOFFS.md` §0/§6, README *Privacy*), the text of the mic and
speech prompts users actually see (`mac/Resources/Info.plist`), and the reason
several design choices look heavier than they need to. The checks in this pack
hold the mechanical half; what follows is the judgment half.

**What may cross the boundary: derived metadata, never audio.** A laugh is
persisted as time, duration, confidence, and a speaker label — that is what the
SQLite rows and the JSONL lines carry. Saved clips (`save_clips`, on by default
in the Python core) are the one place raw audio lands, and it lands on local
disk under the single home directory, never anywhere else. New persisted fields
follow the same split; if a feature wants audio, it belongs in `clips/`, under
the user's existing choice, not in a new location.

**Everything lives in one deletable directory.** `~/.laughcounter` for the Python
core (overridable via `LAUGHCOUNTER_HOME`), `~/Library/Application
Support/LaughCounter/` for the app. "Delete the folder and it's gone" is a
documented property — don't scatter state (caches, model files, logs) outside it.

**The one accepted egress is a model download in an optional extra.** The
`[yamnet]` extra fetches the TF-Hub handle in `detector/yamnet.py`, and the
`[speaker]` extra fetches ECAPA weights from Hugging Face — a one-time download,
made by the ML library, carrying no audio, in a stack the user opted into. The
always-on paths (the native app's Sound Analysis and Speech, the counting/logging
core) need no network at all. Adding a *new* egress means saying so in the README
Privacy section and here, and keeping it out of the capture path.

**The dashboard is unauthenticated — treat every widening as a user decision.**
It binds loopback by default; `--host 0.0.0.0` is the user reaching it from their
phone, and the mutating endpoints require an `application/json` content type so a
browser must preflight cross-origin (`dashboard.py`'s `do_POST`). Any new
mutating endpoint keeps that guard; nothing else stands between the LAN and the
laugh log.

**The disclosure must stay true.** `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription` and
`NSSpeechRecognitionUsageDescription` tell the user audio is analysed on-device
and not recorded. If the app's behaviour ever changes, those strings change with
it in the same commit — a stale privacy prompt is worse than a blunt one.

`NSSpeechRecognitionUsageDescription` tell the user audio is analysed on-device
and not recorded. If the app's behaviour ever changes, those strings change with
it in the same commit — a stale privacy prompt is worse than a blunt one.

input.body:
Prose-to-checks sweep over `.claudinite/local/packs` (the only local pack here is `on-device-privacy`). Two of its prose-only `RULES.md` rules were always-testable; both are checks now.

**This supersedes #51 and #54**, which were two independent runs of the same task. Same two rules, same six files — they differed in how each check detects. This branch takes the stronger half of each; #51 and #54 are closed in its favour. Refs #42, #48.

## `on-device-privacy/json-content-type-guard` (blocking)

RULES.md said *"Any new mutating endpoint keeps that guard"*. Now enforced: every `do_POST` / `do_PUT` / `do_PATCH` / `do_DELETE` in `laughcounter/**.py` must read the **request's own** `Content-Type`, gate on `application/json` in an `if`, and do so *before* reading the body.

Two things make it confident:

- It **parses the handler body by indentation** rather than grepping the file. `dashboard.py` mentions `application/json` eight times as a *response* content type plus once in the inline page's `fetch()`, every one of which would fool a grep. A fixture pins that false alarm — a handler that only *replies* in JSON still fires.
- The content-type read is anchored on `.headers.get("Content-Type")` / `.headers["Content-Type"]`, so `send_header("Content-Type", …)` on the response side can't be mistaken for a guard.

Why blocking: the dashboard has no authentication. The JSON content-type requirement is the only thing forcing a cross-origin browser to preflight, and so the only thing stopping any page the user happens to be visiting from writing to their laugh log. A guard that runs *after* the body read is no guard, which is why ordering is checked too.

## `on-device-privacy/single-home-directory` (blocking)

RULES.md said *"don't scatter state (caches, model files, logs) outside it"*. Now enforced across both implementations:

- **Python** — home-anchored paths in `laughcounter/**.py`: `Path.home()` and `"~/…"` string literals (`expanduser`, `Path(...).expanduser()`) must land under `.laughcounter`. Checking the `Path.home()` *call* rather than only its literal join means `Path.home() / some_var` is caught too.
- **Swift** — `mac/Sources/**.swift` must resolve state via `.applicationSupportDirectory` narrowed with `appendingPathComponent("LaughCounter")`. Any other Foundation standard directory, an un-narrowed Application Support base, or `NSHomeDirectory()` fires. The `urls(for:` scoping keeps unrelated selectors ending in "Directory" (`.createDirectory`, `withIntermediateDirectories`) from tripping it.

One documented **mandated-location exemption**: `cli.py`'s `~/Library/LaunchAgents/{label}.plist`. launchd picks that path, the project doesn't, and `cmd_service` already points the agent's log back at `home_path` — so "delete `~/.laughcounter` and it's gone" still holds. The list is deliberately short: a cache or model directory is a *choice*, and a choice belongs under the home directory.

Absolute paths outside `$HOME` remain prose — the check doesn't claim them, and the trimmed prose says so.

## See-it-fail

`node --test .claudinite/local/packs/on-device-privacy/pack.test.mjs` — **13/13 pass** (7 new). Beyond the fixtures, each check was run against the **real** sources with a realistic regression applied, and each produced exactly one finding (baseline: zero):

- **When there's nothing left to do, say so boldly at the end of the conversation.** Don't bury a "this is complete / I'm blocked / nothing further to do" behind hedging — make the terminal state unmistakable. **Set it apart visually so it catches the eye:** put the terminal state — or, when work remains, the list of open/outstanding items — in its own callout (a Markdown blockquote box, e.g. `> ✅ All done` or `> ⚠️ Still open: …`), not trailing prose the owner has to scan for. One or the other always gets the box: the done-signal when nothing remains, the open-items list when something does.
- **"LGTM"** is the owner's phrase for the merge-to-main command: it asks for the change in front of the owner to be merged into `main`. It's an owner-triggered command; the default mechanics live in the `merge-to-main` skill ([../packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/SKILL.md](../packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/SKILL.md)) (squash, gate on CI only when the repo has it), and a project that diverges overrides them via a bespoke merge-policy file it names in its own `CLAUDE.md`.

- **"Show me the document"** (for a source-controlled document) is the owner's phrase asking for a **link to the document on GitHub** — not the file's contents inlined, and not a local filesystem path. When the document lives in a GitHub-hosted repo, respond with a GitHub link to it (the file on the relevant branch/commit); only fall back to inlining the contents or giving a local path when the document isn't under source control.
- **Put decisions and approvals in an `AskUserQuestion` popup, not buried in prose.** The owner is frequently on mobile, where a popup notifies and a question embedded in a paragraph is easy to miss. When you need the owner to choose or approve something, ask through the structured popup with explicit options rather than asking in running text. **And when several independent items each need a verdict** (a set of proposed fixes, findings to accept), give **each item its own question carrying its own brief case** — the concrete failure, why it matters, the cost of the fix — with per-item approve/defer options; never one bundled choose-a-scope question over the whole set. The owner decides item-wise, from the case, not from a menu of subsets. (The popup carries at most 4 questions per call — split a larger set into consecutive calls.)
- **When asked to produce a prompt or message destined for another context, visually enclose the whole thing.** Any text the owner will lift out and use elsewhere — a prompt for another assistant, a message to send, copy meant to be pasted somewhere — must be set apart as a single delimited block: either a box (e.g. a fenced code block) or fenced top and bottom by two separating lines, so its exact boundaries are unmistakable and it can be copied in one piece. - **Auto-open a PR after committing.** Whenever Claude changes code on a branch and commits it, open a pull request for that branch right after, even without an explicit request to do so. This overrides Claude Code's own default of only opening a PR when explicitly asked.
# Claudinite — active-pack guidance

The baseline plus the packs this project declares. Deeper per-pack reference (e.g. a pack's release doc) is linked from its prose and read on demand.

<!-- pack:basics -->
# Working discipline

The working discipline that isn't itself a GitHub operation — general habits for how to approach a change, independent of any one project.

Start every requested change from the *problem*, not the solution. When the owner asks for a change, don't begin implementing it until the two of you share an explicit understanding of the problem it's meant to solve **and** have agreed that the requested change is the best way to solve it — a different fix, or no change at all, may serve the underlying problem better. Treat the request as a description of a desired outcome, not a specification to execute on sight; surface your read of the problem, raise a better approach if you see one, and reach consensus first. This applies to any repository, not just this one.

An interactive comment from the owner carries one of three build-relevant intents — or none of them — and the classification decides where the change lands and what must exist before any fix. Open your reply to an owner comment with an explicit classification line — `Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other` (`other` covers questions, approvals, and command phrases; a mixed comment names each part) — the assessment itself stays judgment.

1. **A correction** — you misunderstood something. Repair the shared understanding, then rework what the misread already touched — the artifact changes as much as the correction demands; what doesn't appear is a new requirement or rule.
2. **A feature** — a feature run: agree on the requirement, record it in the project's requirements document (its executable spec, where it keeps one), write the test that proves it and watch it fail, then implement until it passes.
3. **A process change** — the owner is changing *how* work is done. The change lands as durable rules in the project's local scope — its own local packs (in Claudinite itself, its packs) — routed through the mechanism promotion ladder (platform setting → hook → check → skill → prose); promoting a rule into the shared canon is the growth lifecycle's separate call, not the interactive session's. Once the intent is understood, author the assurance first: the check the future world must satisfy. Execute it and watch it fail — the failure is the evidence it detects exactly what the owner was worried about — and only then make the fixes that turn it green. When the ladder lands the rule at prose (an in-flight judgment rule no check can carry), the same step is demonstrating the gap: show the corpus doesn't already cover the rule before writing it.

The two build modes share one spine: state the expectation in its durable home first, watch it fail against the current world, then change the world to satisfy it. A fix made before its assurance exists can never show it addressed what the owner actually asked for — and an unrouted comment tends to become a one-off patch where a requirement or a rule should have accumulated.

Confirm a behavior isn't already provided before building a mechanism for it — verify the gap against a real run first; the cheapest fix is often that it already works.

When feedback flags a misunderstanding, don't reflexively expand the artifact to compensate. First check whether it's already correct — if it is, say so and push back rather than editing; a misread doesn't imply the text is wrong (the sibling of the rule above). And size writing to its idea: "open one issue" takes a sentence, not three paragraphs — prose padded to preempt confusion usually breeds it.

When correcting or auditing an artifact against an authoritative source, derive the corrected version from the *source* before reading the existing draft — reading the draft first anchors you to its framing and quietly carries its errors into your "fix." Build from the source, then diff against the old draft to surface what was actually wrong; a clean-room rebuild catches biases an edit-in-place pass silently inherits.

Fix build/test/CI warnings, don't tolerate them: a clean run with no warnings makes a genuinely new warning or error stand out, so noise here costs detection later. Prefer a small, targeted fix that addresses the *cause* in the same change.

Suppressing a warning — muting it with a flag (e.g. `--disable-warning`), `eslint-disable`, swallowing it, etc. — is **not** a small fix: it hides the signal instead of resolving it. Never reach for suppression as the quick path — it's only ever a deliberate, reviewed decision, made once the real fix has been weighed and rejected, never an unattended default. A suppression you do keep must **carry its reason at the site**: an explanation on the suppression line, or in the comment immediately above it, saying why the fix was rejected. That inline reason *is* the review record — it's what separates a considered suppression from a reflexive mute, and it's why the suppression needs no second justification recorded elsewhere.

Before working around a finding from a vendored check, confirm the vendored copy is current. It reflects its last refresh, not upstream's head, so the fix may already exist upstream and simply not be pulled in yet.

When a warning can't be fixed with a small cause-addressing change now without hindering current work (e.g. it's waiting on an upstream release, or the real fix is a larger refactor), open a dedicated issue for it (unless one is already open) so it's tracked and not lost — then move on. Resolving it (real fix, or a consciously-chosen suppression) happens in that issue's own change.

An approval — to merge, to ship, to proceed — applies only *backward*, to the work already in front of the owner when it's given, never to anything requested or done *after* it. A later follow-up, even a fix to the just-approved change, needs its own explicit approval; don't carry one approval forward, and don't treat a chosen answer to a multiple-choice prompt as authorization just because an option's wording mentioned the action. When in doubt, surface the new state and wait for a fresh approval.

# The task lifecycle

The issue → branch → PR lifecycle every new task follows, independent of any one project; this section keeps the method. The rest of the git/GitHub procedures live in the `git-github-advanced` skill.

For every new task:

1. Create a GitHub issue describing the task before starting work.
2. Develop on a branch; reference that issue number in commit messages (e.g. `Refs #123`, `Fixes #123`, or `Closes #123`).
3. Update the issue's status (comments / close) as work progresses and when it's done.

The nightly PR/branch/issue sweep, active wherever this pack is declared. The fleet routine runs the
pack's one maintenance task (`repo-tidy`) against a repo; this is the policy it follows. The per-object
**method** lives in the pack's skills ([single-branch-status](skills/single-branch-status/SKILL.md),

- **Branches, PRs — assess only.** They may be work in progress. Report which should stay and which
  are safe to close/delete; **never** delete, push, merge, or close them. Judge by *content* (the
  landed-status test), never a ref's auto-generated name.
- **Issues — act.** Take the first applicable action: close-if-implemented / needs-decision / blocked
  / quick-win / leave. "Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s
  content **now** — confirm it there and cite it; when you can't, comment, don't close. Every action
  defaults to the reversible option (comment / leave) when the check is inconclusive.

The `repo-tidy` pass applies each single-object skill across the targets the plan hands it, then
rewrites the repo's standing tracker from the verdicts it gathered (one issue per repo, body rewritten

# On-device privacy — the boundary the whole product is built around

An always-on microphone in someone's living room only earns its place if what it
hears stays on the machine. That promise is the product requirement
(`docs/DESIGN-AND-TRADEOFFS.md` §0/§6, README *Privacy*), the text of the mic and
speech prompts users actually see (`mac/Resources/Info.plist`), and the reason
several design choices look heavier than they need to. The checks in this pack
hold the mechanical half; what follows is the judgment half.

**What may cross the boundary: derived metadata, never audio.** A laugh is
persisted as time, duration, confidence, and a speaker label — that is what the
SQLite rows and the JSONL lines carry. Saved clips (`save_clips`, on by default
in the Python core) are the one place raw audio lands, and it lands on local
disk under the single home directory, never anywhere else. New persisted fields
follow the same split; if a feature wants audio, it belongs in `clips/`, under
the user's existing choice, not in a new location.

**Everything lives in one deletable directory.** The two locations and the "no
state outside them" rule are the `single-home-directory` check's job now. What it
can't hold: "delete the folder and it's gone" is a promise a user *acts on* —
someone who deletes it believes the mic's whole memory of them went with it. So a
feature that needs somewhere new to keep things moves or extends the one home
directory rather than earning a second one, and the launchd plist stays the sole
exception because macOS, not us, chose where it goes. Absolute paths outside
`$HOME` are still yours to judge; the check doesn't claim them.

**The one accepted egress is a model download in an optional extra.** The
`[yamnet]` extra fetches the TF-Hub handle in `detector/yamnet.py`, and the
`[speaker]` extra fetches ECAPA weights from Hugging Face — a one-time download,
made by the ML library, carrying no audio, in a stack the user opted into. The
always-on paths (the native app's Sound Analysis and Speech, the counting/logging
core) need no network at all. Adding a *new* egress means saying so in the README
Privacy section and here, and keeping it out of the capture path.

**The dashboard is unauthenticated — treat every widening as a user decision.**
Both mechanical halves are checks: `loopback-default` for the bind address,
`json-content-type-guard` for the mutating handlers' cross-origin preflight. What
stays judgment is that those two *are* the entire defence — the content-type
requirement is doing more work than it looks like, since forcing a preflight is
the whole CSRF story here, and `--host 0.0.0.0` is a user reaching their own
dashboard from their phone, never a default to drift toward. Nothing else stands
between the LAN, or a page the user happens to be visiting, and the laugh log, so
a new capability on that surface is a fresh exposure decision, not a routine
endpoint.

**The disclosure must stay true.** `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription` and
`NSSpeechRecognitionUsageDescription` tell the user audio is analysed on-device
and not recorded. If the app's behaviour ever changes, those strings change with
it in the same commit — a stale privacy prompt is worse than a blunt one.

Comment class: other — a validation question; assessment below, no changes made.

## Where this PR came from

Nobody asked for a feature. This repo runs "Claudinite," and one of its standing automations is a **prose-to-checks sweep** (tracker #42): a scheduled GitHub-Actions-spawned agent task that mines the repo's own local pack prose (`RULES.md`) for rules that are mechanically testable but only enforced by prose, and converts them to automated checks via a PR a human must approve. That task fired on July 27 (#48 → PR 51) and again July 28 (→ PR 54), each run unaware of the other — hence the duplicates you asked me to merge. So the honest framing is: **this is the meta-system generating guardrail work for itself**, and the right question is exactly the one you asked — is the guardrail worth having?

## What it actually adds

Two lint-style checks (~380 lines including tests) that run in the repo's existing `check_the_world`/`check_the_work` gates:

1. **`json-content-type-guard`** — every mutating HTTP handler in `laughcounter/` must reject non-`application/json` requests before reading the body.
2. **`single-home-directory`** — persisted state must land in `~/.laughcounter` (Python) or `Application Support/LaughCounter` (Swift), nowhere else.

Plus trimming the two RULES.md paragraphs those checks now cover.

## Are the underlying claims real?

I re-verified the security claim from the actual code rather than the PR text, and it holds. `dashboard.py` is an **unauthenticated** server whose `do_POST` writes to the database (`/api/mark` inserts laughs, `/api/label` relabels/deletes rows). Any web page you visit can fire a POST at `[REDACTED:env:CLOUDSDK_PROXY_ADDRESS]:8422` — browsers allow that cross-origin for "simple" requests (forms, `text/plain` fetch) with no preflight. The *only* thing blocking that today is the content-type check at `laughcounter/dashboard.py:61-64`: requiring `application/json` makes the request non-simple, forcing a CORS preflight the server never approves. Delete those four lines and every page in the user's browser gets a silent write handle on the laugh log — **and no test or observable behavior breaks**. That "regression is silent" property is the strongest genuine argument for a mechanical check.

The home-directory rule guards a documented promise ("delete `~/.laughcounter` and it's gone") but a violation is lower-stakes — stale data survives a delete, not remote writability.

## The honest case against

- **Today it guards one handler and about five path sites.** All value is in catching *future* regressions. In a human-reviewed repo I'd call that thin; here, most code is agent-written on scheduled tasks with a light review loop, which is precisely the environment where a dropped four-line guard slips through — that materially raises the value.
- **The checks are brittle heuristics.** If someone refactors the guard into a helper (`self._require_json()`), or builds paths through indirection, the checks false-positive and must be amended. That's real ongoing maintenance cost, and these are hand-rolled indentation/regex parsers, not real AST analysis.
- **The prose edits are a mild loss.** The original RULES.md paragraphs stated the rules directly; the replacements are meta-commentary about what the checks do and don't cover. Readable, but less crisp than what they replaced.

## Bottom line

The mechanism is sound and the code does what it claims (13/13 fixtures, and I mutation-tested it against the real sources). On the merits: **`json-content-type-guard` earns its keep** — it pins the repo's only CSRF defence, whose failure mode is silent, in a codebase mostly written by agents. **`single-home-directory` is marginal** — defensible, but I'd not have flagged it as must-have; blocking severity is arguably too strong for what's partly a tidiness rule. And if you don't buy the prose-to-checks premise at all, the thing to change is the Claudinite growth routine that generates this class of PR — closing #55 alone just means the next sweep proposes it again.

> ⚠️ Your call on #55: (a) LGTM as-is, (b) merge with `single-home-directory` dropped or demoted to advisory, or (c) close it and I'll note in tracker #42 that this conversion was reviewed and declined so future sweeps skip it.

# On-device privacy — the boundary the whole product is built around

An always-on microphone in someone's living room only earns its place if what it
hears stays on the machine. That promise is the product requirement
(`docs/DESIGN-AND-TRADEOFFS.md` §0/§6, README *Privacy*), the text of the mic and
speech prompts users actually see (`mac/Resources/Info.plist`), and the reason
several design choices look heavier than they need to. The checks in this pack
hold the mechanical half; what follows is the judgment half.

**What may cross the boundary: derived metadata, never audio.** A laugh is
persisted as time, duration, confidence, and a speaker label — that is what the
SQLite rows and the JSONL lines carry. Saved clips (`save_clips`, on by default
in the Python core) are the one place raw audio lands, and it lands on local
disk under the single home directory, never anywhere else. New persisted fields
follow the same split; if a feature wants audio, it belongs in `clips/`, under
the user's existing choice, not in a new location.

**Everything lives in one deletable directory.** `~/.laughcounter` for the Python
core (overridable via `LAUGHCOUNTER_HOME`), `~/Library/Application
Support/LaughCounter/` for the app. "Delete the folder and it's gone" is a
documented property — don't scatter state (caches, model files, logs) outside it.

**The one accepted egress is a model download in an optional extra.** The
`[yamnet]` extra fetches the TF-Hub handle in `detector/yamnet.py`, and the
`[speaker]` extra fetches ECAPA weights from Hugging Face — a one-time download,
made by the ML library, carrying no audio, in a stack the user opted into. The
always-on paths (the native app's Sound Analysis and Speech, the counting/logging
core) need no network at all. Adding a *new* egress means saying so in the README
Privacy section and here, and keeping it out of the capture path.

**The dashboard is unauthenticated — treat every widening as a user decision.**
It binds loopback by default; `--host 0.0.0.0` is the user reaching it from their
phone, and the mutating endpoints require an `application/json` content type so a
browser must preflight cross-origin (`dashboard.py`'s `do_POST`). Any new
mutating endpoint keeps that guard; nothing else stands between the LAN and the
laugh log.

**The disclosure must stay true.** `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription` and
`NSSpeechRecognitionUsageDescription` tell the user audio is analysed on-device
and not recorded. If the app's behaviour ever changes, those strings change with
it in the same commit — a stale privacy prompt is worse than a blunt one.

# on-device-privacy

LaughCounter's defining constraint as a local pack: an always-on living-room microphone whose audio
never leaves the machine. Distilled from this repo's own sources and requirements
(`docs/DESIGN-AND-TRADEOFFS.md` §0/§6, the README *Privacy* section, `laughcounter/`,
`mac/Sources/LaughCounter/`) — the promise was stated in three docs and enforced nowhere.

Local pack, declared by hand as `local/on-device-privacy` (no fingerprint). It spans both
implementations, because the boundary is the same on either side of them.

| Rule | How enforced |
| --- | --- |
| No outbound client in capture path | `no-network-client` check (`laughcounter/**.py`, `mac/Sources/**.swift`) |
| Dashboard binds loopback | `loopback-default` check (host defaults in `laughcounter/`) |
| Mutating endpoints require JSON | `json-content-type-guard` check (`do_POST`/`PUT`/`PATCH`/`DELETE` bodies) |
| Speech recognition on-device | `on-device-speech` check (`SFSpeechAudioBufferRecognitionRequest`) |
| One deletable home directory | `single-home-directory` check (home-anchored paths, Foundation standard dirs) |
| Metadata persists, audio doesn't | `RULES.md` prose |
| Model download is the only egress | `RULES.md` prose |
| Usage strings stay true | `RULES.md` prose |

Fixtures: `pack.test.mjs` — `node --test .claudinite/local/packs/on-device-privacy/pack.test.mjs`.
Each check has a violating fixture it fires on and the repo's real files it stays quiet on. They sit
in the pack, not in `tests/`, because a consumer file may not reference into `.claudinite/`
(the `claudinite-isolation` barrier).

input.title: on-device-privacy: convert the mutating-endpoint JSON guard from prose to a check
input.body:
Prose-to-checks conversion over the `on-device-privacy` local pack, reduced after owner review to the one rule that earns a blocking check.

**Supersedes #51 and #54** (two independent runs of the same sweep; this branch merges the stronger detection half of each). The `single-home-directory` check both of them also proposed was reviewed and **dropped** — partly a tidiness rule, not worth a blocking bespoke analyzer; it stays prose. Refs #42, #48.

## `on-device-privacy/json-content-type-guard` (blocking)

The dashboard is an unauthenticated local HTTP server whose `do_POST` writes to the database. Any web page the user visits can send a cross-origin POST to `[REDACTED:env:CLOUDSDK_PROXY_ADDRESS]:8422` — browsers allow that without asking, as long as the request is "simple" (form encoding, `text/plain`). Requiring `Content-Type: application/json` makes the request non-simple, which forces the browser to send a CORS preflight the dashboard never approves — so the write is blocked. That four-line guard in `do_POST` is the dashboard's entire CSRF defence, and deleting it breaks no test and changes no visible behavior. This check makes that silent regression loud.

Enforced: every `do_POST` / `do_PUT` / `do_PATCH` / `do_DELETE` in `laughcounter/**.py` must read the **request's own** `Content-Type`, gate on `application/json` in an `if`, and do so *before* reading the body (a guard after the body read is no guard).

What makes the detection confident:

- It **parses the handler body by indentation** rather than grepping the file. `dashboard.py` mentions `application/json` eight times as a *response* content type plus once in the inline page's `fetch()` — every one would fool a grep. A fixture pins that false alarm.
- The content-type read is anchored on `.headers.get("Content-Type")` / `.headers["Content-Type"]`, so `send_header("Content-Type", …)` on the response side can't be mistaken for a guard.

## See-it-fail

`node --test .claudinite/local/packs/on-device-privacy/pack.test.mjs` — **10/10 pass** (4 new). Beyond the fixtures, the check was run against the **real** `dashboard.py` with a realistic regression applied, each producing exactly one finding (baseline: zero):

| Mutation to real source | Finding |
| --- | --- |
| content-type guard deleted | `do_POST()` mutates without requiring `application/json` |
| body read hoisted above the guard | `do_POST()` reads the body before checking the type |
| unguarded `do_DELETE` added | `do_DELETE()` mutates without requiring `application/json` |

`check_the_world` and `check_the_work` both exit 0 with the rule registered.

## Left as prose

- *One deletable home directory* — reviewed and deliberately left prose (see above); `RULES.md`'s original paragraph is restored verbatim.
- *Metadata persists, audio doesn't* — a judgment about a field's meaning, not a static signature.
- *The model download is the only accepted egress* — the negative half is already `no-network-client`; the positive half is a decision, not a condition.
- *The disclosure must stay true* — the enforceable version (the strings exist) is a weaker, different rule than the prose's (they change in the same commit as the behaviour).

## Surface

The rule module, one line in `pack.mjs`, its fixtures, the trimmed dashboard paragraph in `RULES.md`, and the README enforcement-table row. Nothing outside `.claudinite/local/packs/on-device-privacy/`.

Left open for review — a new blocking check is exactly the thing that shouldn't self-merge.

Done — `single-home-directory` is gone from #55 (rule, tests, prose edits all reverted; the original RULES.md paragraph is back verbatim). The PR is now just the one check: 10/10 tests, both repo gates green, title and body rewritten to match.

## json-content-type-guard, explained differently

Forget the check for a second — here's the underlying problem it protects.

**The setup.** When you run `laughcounter dashboard`, your Mac runs a tiny web server at `[REDACTED:env:CLOUDSDK_PROXY_ADDRESS]:8422`. It has no login, no password, no cookies — anyone who can send it an HTTP request can use it. That includes `POST /api/label`, which can relabel or delete rows in your laugh database.

**The attack.** "Anyone who can send it a request" includes *your own browser* — and your browser takes orders from whatever page you have open. If you visit `random-blog.com` while the dashboard is running, that page's JavaScript can say "send a POST to `http://[REDACTED:env:CLOUDSDK_PROXY_ADDRESS]:8422/api/label`," and your browser will happily deliver it — from the blog straight to the server on your machine. The blog can't *read* the reply, but it doesn't need to: the damage is that the write goes through. This is classic CSRF.

**The one thing in the way.** Browsers sort cross-site requests into two bins. "Simple" requests (form submissions, `text/plain` bodies) are sent immediately, no questions asked. Anything fancier — including a body labeled `Content-Type: application/json` — makes the browser stop and first ask the target server for permission (the CORS "preflight"). Our dashboard never grants that permission, so the browser refuses to send the real request.

The trick: the dashboard's `do_POST` **rejects every request that isn't labeled `application/json`**. That forces attackers into the fancy bin. A malicious page now has two options — send a "simple" request that arrives but gets bounced with a 415, or send a JSON request that the browser itself refuses to deliver. Either way, no write. (You, using the dashboard normally, are unaffected — same-origin requests never need preflight.)

**Why a check.** The entire defence is four lines inside `do_POST` (`dashboard.py:61-64`). Delete them and nothing complains — every test passes, the dashboard works exactly the same, laughs get counted. The only change is invisible: any web page can now write to your laugh log. Code whose removal is silent is exactly what a mechanical check is for. This one fails the build if any mutating handler is missing that content-type rejection, or does it only after already reading the request body.

> ⚠️ Still open: #55 — now the single `json-content-type-guard` check — awaits your review. Say LGTM to merge, or close it and I'll log the decision in tracker #42.

# Claudinite — active-pack guidance

The baseline plus the packs this project declares. Deeper per-pack reference (e.g. a pack's release doc) is linked from its prose and read on demand.

<!-- pack:basics -->
# Working discipline

The working discipline that isn't itself a GitHub operation — general habits for how to approach a change, independent of any one project.

Start every requested change from the *problem*, not the solution. When the owner asks for a change, don't begin implementing it until the two of you share an explicit understanding of the problem it's meant to solve **and** have agreed that the requested change is the best way to solve it — a different fix, or no change at all, may serve the underlying problem better. Treat the request as a description of a desired outcome, not a specification to execute on sight; surface your read of the problem, raise a better approach if you see one, and reach consensus first. This applies to any repository, not just this one.

An interactive comment from the owner carries one of three build-relevant intents — or none of them — and the classification decides where the change lands and what must exist before any fix. Open your reply to an owner comment with an explicit classification line — `Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other` (`other` covers questions, approvals, and command phrases; a mixed comment names each part) — the assessment itself stays judgment.

1. **A correction** — you misunderstood something. Repair the shared understanding, then rework what the misread already touched — the artifact changes as much as the correction demands; what doesn't appear is a new requirement or rule.
2. **A feature** — a feature run: agree on the requirement, record it in the project's requirements document (its executable spec, where it keeps one), write the test that proves it and watch it fail, then implement until it passes.
3. **A process change** — the owner is changing *how* work is done. The change lands as durable rules in the project's local scope — its own local packs (in Claudinite itself, its packs) — routed through the mechanism promotion ladder (platform setting → hook → check → skill → prose); promoting a rule into the shared canon is the growth lifecycle's separate call, not the interactive session's. Once the intent is understood, author the assurance first: the check the future world must satisfy. Execute it and watch it fail — the failure is the evidence it detects exactly what the owner was worried about — and only then make the fixes that turn it green. When the ladder lands the rule at prose (an in-flight judgment rule no check can carry), the same step is demonstrating the gap: show the corpus doesn't already cover the rule before writing it.

The two build modes share one spine: state the expectation in its durable home first, watch it fail against the current world, then change the world to satisfy it. A fix made before its assurance exists can never show it addressed what the owner actually asked for — and an unrouted comment tends to become a one-off patch where a requirement or a rule should have accumulated.

Confirm a behavior isn't already provided before building a mechanism for it — verify the gap against a real run first; the cheapest fix is often that it already works.

When feedback flags a misunderstanding, don't reflexively expand the artifact to compensate. First check whether it's already correct — if it is, say so and push back rather than editing; a misread doesn't imply the text is wrong (the sibling of the rule above). And size writing to its idea: "open one issue" takes a sentence, not three paragraphs — prose padded to preempt confusion usually breeds it.

When correcting or auditing an artifact against an authoritative source, derive the corrected version from the *source* before reading the existing draft — reading the draft first anchors you to its framing and quietly carries its errors into your "fix." Build from the source, then diff against the old draft to surface what was actually wrong; a clean-room rebuild catches biases an edit-in-place pass silently inherits.

Fix build/test/CI warnings, don't tolerate them: a clean run with no warnings makes a genuinely new warning or error stand out, so noise here costs detection later. Prefer a small, targeted fix that addresses the *cause* in the same change.

Suppressing a warning — muting it with a flag (e.g. `--disable-warning`), `eslint-disable`, swallowing it, etc. — is **not** a small fix: it hides the signal instead of resolving it. Never reach for suppression as the quick path — it's only ever a deliberate, reviewed decision, made once the real fix has been weighed and rejected, never an unattended default. A suppression you do keep must **carry its reason at the site**: an explanation on the suppression line, or in the comment immediately above it, saying why the fix was rejected. That inline reason *is* the review record — it's what separates a considered suppression from a reflexive mute, and it's why the suppression needs no second justification recorded elsewhere.

Before working around a finding from a vendored check, confirm the vendored copy is current. It reflects its last refresh, not upstream's head, so the fix may already exist upstream and simply not be pulled in yet.

When a warning can't be fixed with a small cause-addressing change now without hindering current work (e.g. it's waiting on an upstream release, or the real fix is a larger refactor), open a dedicated issue for it (unless one is already open) so it's tracked and not lost — then move on. Resolving it (real fix, or a consciously-chosen suppression) happens in that issue's own change.

An approval — to merge, to ship, to proceed — applies only *backward*, to the work already in front of the owner when it's given, never to anything requested or done *after* it. A later follow-up, even a fix to the just-approved change, needs its own explicit approval; don't carry one approval forward, and don't treat a chosen answer to a multiple-choice prompt as authorization just because an option's wording mentioned the action. When in doubt, surface the new state and wait for a fresh approval.

# The task lifecycle

The issue → branch → PR lifecycle every new task follows, independent of any one project; this section keeps the method. The rest of the git/GitHub procedures live in the `git-github-advanced` skill.

For every new task:

1. Create a GitHub issue describing the task before starting work.
2. Develop on a branch; reference that issue number in commit messages (e.g. `Refs #123`, `Fixes #123`, or `Closes #123`).
3. Update the issue's status (comments / close) as work progresses and when it's done.

# tidy-repo — the repo tidy-up policy

The nightly PR/branch/issue sweep, active wherever this pack is declared. The fleet routine runs the
pack's one maintenance task (`repo-tidy`) against a repo; this is the policy it follows. The per-object
**method** lives in the pack's skills ([single-branch-status](skills/single-branch-status/SKILL.md),
[single-pr-status](skills/single-pr-status/SKILL.md),
[single-issue-triage](skills/single-issue-triage/SKILL.md)); the same task also reconciles the
standing tracker at the end of its pass.

The one rule that shapes everything: **assess PRs and branches read-only; act only on issues.**

- **Branches, PRs — assess only.** They may be work in progress. Report which should stay and which
  are safe to close/delete; **never** delete, push, merge, or close them. Judge by *content* (the
  landed-status test), never a ref's auto-generated name.
- **Issues — act.** Take the first applicable action: close-if-implemented / needs-decision / blocked
  / quick-win / leave. "Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s
  content **now** — confirm it there and cite it; when you can't, comment, don't close. Every action
  defaults to the reversible option (comment / leave) when the check is inconclusive.

The `repo-tidy` pass applies each single-object skill across the targets the plan hands it, then
rewrites the repo's standing tracker from the verdicts it gathered (one issue per repo, body rewritten
to today's state, a dated comment per run).

<!-- pack:on-device-privacy -->
# On-device privacy — the boundary the whole product is built around

An always-on microphone in someone's living room only earns its place if what it
hears stays on the machine. That promise is the product requirement
(`docs/DESIGN-AND-TRADEOFFS.md` §0/§6, README *Privacy*), the text of the mic and
speech prompts users actually see (`mac/Resources/Info.plist`), and the reason
several design choices look heavier than they need to. The checks in this pack
hold the mechanical half; what follows is the judgment half.

**What may cross the boundary: derived metadata, never audio.** A laugh is
persisted as time, duration, confidence, and a speaker label — that is what the
SQLite rows and the JSONL lines carry. Saved clips (`save_clips`, on by default
in the Python core) are the one place raw audio lands, and it lands on local
disk under the single home directory, never anywhere else. New persisted fields
follow the same split; if a feature wants audio, it belongs in `clips/`, under
the user's existing choice, not in a new location.

**Everything lives in one deletable directory.** `~/.laughcounter` for the Python
core (overridable via `LAUGHCOUNTER_HOME`), `~/Library/Application
Support/LaughCounter/` for the app. "Delete the folder and it's gone" is a
documented property — don't scatter state (caches, model files, logs) outside it.

**The one accepted egress is a model download in an optional extra.** The
`[yamnet]` extra fetches the TF-Hub handle in `detector/yamnet.py`, and the
`[speaker]` extra fetches ECAPA weights from Hugging Face — a one-time download,
made by the ML library, carrying no audio, in a stack the user opted into. The
always-on paths (the native app's Sound Analysis and Speech, the counting/logging
core) need no network at all. Adding a *new* egress means saying so in the README
Privacy section and here, and keeping it out of the capture path.

**The dashboard is unauthenticated — treat every widening as a user decision.**
It binds loopback by default; `--host 0.0.0.0` is the user reaching it from their
phone, never a default to drift toward. The mutating handlers' `application/json`
requirement is held by the `json-content-type-guard` check now; what stays
judgment is that the bind address and that guard *are* the entire defence —
nothing else stands between the LAN, or a page the user happens to be visiting,
and the laugh log. A new capability on that surface is a fresh exposure decision,
not a routine endpoint.

**The disclosure must stay true.** `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription` and
`NSSpeechRecognitionUsageDescription` tell the user audio is analysed on-device
and not recorded. If the app's behaviour ever changes, those strings change with
it in the same commit — a stale privacy prompt is worse than a blunt one.

content.text:
**The port isn't open by default — it's opt-in.** The server only exists while you run `laughcounter serve`; it's a separate CLI command (`laughcounter/cli.py:331`), not something the counter starts on its own. Just running the counter opens no port at all. And when you do run it, it binds `[REDACTED:env:CLOUDSDK_PROXY_ADDRESS]`, so only your own machine can reach it unless you explicitly pass `--host 0.0.0.0`.

**What it's for** — it's the product's viewing and feedback surface. LaughCounter itself is a headless always-on mic pipeline (mic → detector → counter → SQLite). The dashboard is how you actually *see* and *correct* what it counted, from a browser — deliberately phone-friendly, per the README, so you can glance at it from the couch:

- **`GET /`** — an HTML page with your laugh stats (today's count, history, recent detections).
- **`POST /api/mark`** — the "that was a laugh, you missed it" button: manually logs a laugh (yours or a guest's). If a near-miss detection was close by, it confirms it instead of double-counting.
- **`POST /api/label`** — the opposite correction: "not a laugh" on a false detection, or relabeling who laughed. This is the feedback loop the README describes for tuning the detector against your actual living room.

So the two POST endpoints exist because correcting the log *from your phone* is a core workflow — and that's also exactly why they're mutating, unauthenticated, and worth the CSRF guard from #55: the intended user taps buttons on the served page (same-origin, no preflight needed), while any other page in any browser gets bounced.

One nuance worth having straight: the CSRF risk exists even in the loopback-only default — the attack rides *your* browser, which sits on the same machine as the server, so `[REDACTED:env:CLOUDSDK_PROXY_ADDRESS]` doesn't block it. That's why the content-type guard is the load-bearing piece rather than the bind address.

> ⚠️ Still open: #55 (`json-content-type-guard`) awaits your review — LGTM to merge, or close and I'll log the decline in tracker #42.

7	
8	Local pack, declared by hand as `local/on-device-privacy` (no fingerprint). It spans both
9	implementations, because the boundary is the same on either side of them.
10	
11	| Rule | How enforced |
12	| --- | --- |
13	| No outbound client in capture path | `no-network-client` check (`laughcounter/**.py`, `mac/Sources/**.swift`) |
14	| Dashboard binds loopback | `loopback-default` check (host defaults in `laughcounter/`) |
15	| Speech recognition on-device | `on-device-speech` check (`SFSpeechAudioBufferRecognitionRequest`) |
16	| Metadata persists, audio doesn't | `RULES.md` prose |
17	| One deletable home directory | `RULES.md` prose |
18	| Model download is the only egress | `RULES.md` prose |
19	| Usage strings stay true | `RULES.md` prose |
20	
21	Fixtures: `pack.test.mjs` — `node --test .claudinite/local/packs/on-device-privacy/pack.test.mjs`.
22	Each check has a violating fixture it fires on and the repo's real files it stays quiet on. They sit

1	import noNetworkClient from './no-network-client.mjs';
2	import loopbackDefault from './loopback-default.mjs';
3	import onDeviceSpeech from './on-device-speech.mjs';
4	
5	// LaughCounter's defining constraint, as a pack: an always-on microphone in the
6	// living room, and the promise that what it hears never leaves the machine. The
7	// product requirements (docs/DESIGN-AND-TRADEOFFS.md §0/§6) and the README's
8	// Privacy section state it; nothing enforced it until this pack. It spans both
9	// implementations — the Python reference (laughcounter/) and the native app
10	// (mac/Sources/) — because the boundary is the same on both sides.
11	//
12	// A local pack: declared by hand as `local/on-device-privacy`, never
13	// fingerprinted (detect/marker null).
14	export default {
15	  id: 'on-device-privacy',
16	  detect: null,
17	  marker: null,
18	  prose: 'RULES.md',
19	  rules: [noNetworkClient, loopbackDefault, onDeviceSpeech],
20	};

25	`[speaker]` extra fetches ECAPA weights from Hugging Face — a one-time download,
26	made by the ML library, carrying no audio, in a stack the user opted into. The
27	always-on paths (the native app's Sound Analysis and Speech, the counting/logging
28	core) need no network at all. Adding a *new* egress means saying so in the README
29	Privacy section and here, and keeping it out of the capture path.
30	
31	**The dashboard is unauthenticated — treat every widening as a user decision.**
32	It binds loopback by default; `--host 0.0.0.0` is the user reaching it from their
33	phone, and the mutating endpoints require an `application/json` content type so a
34	browser must preflight cross-origin (`dashboard.py`'s `do_POST`). Any new
35	mutating endpoint keeps that guard; nothing else stands between the LAN and the
36	laugh log.
37	
38	**The disclosure must stay true.** `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription` and
39	`NSSpeechRecognitionUsageDescription` tell the user audio is analysed on-device
40	and not recorded. If the app's behaviour ever changes, those strings change with
41	it in the same commit — a stale privacy prompt is worse than a blunt one.

"""Command-line interface for LaughCounter.

Subcommands:
    listen    Listen to the microphone and log laughs (needs the [yamnet] extra).
    simulate  Generate synthetic laughs to try out the whole pipeline offline.
    stats     Print a summary of your laughter.
    log       Show the most recent laughs.
    export    Dump all events as CSV or JSON.
    serve     Launch the local web dashboard.
    config    Show or initialise configuration.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# stats / log / export / serve / config
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def cmd_stats(args, cfg: Config) -> int:
        print(f"Exported {len(rows)} event(s) → {args.out}")
    else:
        sys.stdout.write(text)
    return 0


def cmd_serve(args, cfg: Config) -> int:
    from .dashboard import serve

    host = args.host or cfg.dashboard_host
    port = args.port or cfg.dashboard_port
    # Ensure the database exists so the first page load has a table to read.
    Storage(cfg.db_path, cfg.jsonl_path).close()
    serve(cfg.db_path, host=host, port=port, jsonl_path=cfg.jsonl_path)
    return 0


def cmd_mark(args, cfg: Config) -> int:
    who = "guest" if args.guest else "me"
    store = Storage(cfg.db_path, cfg.jsonl_path)
    result = store.mark(now=utcnow(), who=who, window=cfg.mark_window)
    s.set_defaults(func=cmd_log)

    s = sub.add_parser("export", help="export all events")
    s.add_argument("--format", choices=["csv", "json"], default="csv")
    s.add_argument("--out", help="output file (default: stdout)")
    s.set_defaults(func=cmd_export)

    s = sub.add_parser("serve", help="run the local web dashboard")
    s.add_argument("--host", help="bind address (default [REDACTED:env:CLOUDSDK_PROXY_ADDRESS])")
    s.add_argument("--port", type=int, help="port (default 8422)")
    s.set_defaults(func=cmd_serve)

    s = sub.add_parser("config", help="show or initialise configuration")
    s.add_argument("--init", action="store_true", help="write a default config file")
    s.set_defaults(func=cmd_config)

"""Tests for the feedback loop: mark, relabel, speaker correction, migration."""

import sqlite3

import pytest

from laughcounter.events import LaughEvent
from laughcounter.storage import Storage, apply_label, apply_mark


def make_event(start, dur=1.0, speaker="unknown"):
    return LaughEvent(start=start, end=start + dur, duration=dur,
                      peak_score=0.8, mean_score=0.6, source="mic", speaker=speaker)

def test_set_label_and_speaker_validation(tmp_path):
    store = Storage(tmp_path / "l.db")
    rid = store.add(make_event(1.0))
    assert store.set_label(rid, "rejected") is True
    assert store.get(rid)["label"] == "rejected"
    assert store.set_speaker(rid, "guest") is True
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        store.set_label(rid, "bogus")
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        store.set_speaker(rid, "nobody")
    assert store.set_label(9999, "rejected") is False  # no such row
    store.close()


def test_apply_helpers_are_standalone(tmp_path):
    db = tmp_path / "l.db"
    Storage(db).close()  # create schema
    res = apply_mark(db, who="me", now=1000.0)
    assert res["action"] == "missed"
    rid = res["id"]
    r2 = apply_label(db, rid, "reject")
    assert r2["ok"] is True
    r3 = apply_label(db, rid, "guest")
    assert r3["ok"] is True
    with pytest.raises(ValueError):
        apply_label(db, rid, "nonsense")


def test_rejected_excluded_from_counts(tmp_path):
    store = Storage(tmp_path / "l.db")
    a = store.add(make_event(1.0))

import json

from laughcounter.events import LaughEvent

def test_add_and_read_back(tmp_path):
    db = tmp_path / "l.db"

## How it works

```
 USB/webcam mic ─► detector ─► counter ─► storage ─► stats / dashboard
  (living room)   (YAMNet)    (state      (SQLite +   (CLI + phone-friendly
                              machine)     clips)      web page + feedback)
       │                                     ▲
       └──── short clip saved per laugh ──────┘  (to improve accuracy over time)

   laugh.
4. **Feedback** — a soft blip tells you it caught one; if it missed, one tap logs
   the miss as training data.

The core (counting, storage, stats, dashboard, feedback, CLI) needs **only the
Python standard library**. TensorFlow, the mic, and the speaker model are optional
extras used only for live listening.

---


# 3. Try it (Ctrl+C to stop). Laugh at it!
```
